title: Simulating surveys with spatially varying detectability
text:
In the RMNP survey, moose were harder to detect under dense canopy: the detection function with canopy cover (pabove2) was clearly better supported than one without it. Detectability therefore varies across the landscape, and so does the proportion of animals a survey misses. Whether this matters depends on the design. A design across the whole park samples all canopy conditions in proportion to their area, but subplots may by chance fall in denser or more open forest than the park as a whole.
Simulations normally draw detectability from a fixed detection function, or from individual covariates such as group size that are unrelated to location. The fork of dsims adds spatial covariates: make.detectability() takes a raster through the new cov.surface argument, and at every repetition reads the raster at each simulated animal’s location. The animal’s scale parameter is then
\[\log(\sigma_i) = \log(\sigma_0) + \beta z_i,\]
where \(z_i\) is the raster value at the animal, \(\beta\) the coefficient in cov.param, and \(\sigma_0\) the scale parameter. This is the same log-linear form that Distance uses for covariates, so the fitted coefficients can be used directly. This article is the first documentation of the feature.

title: Simulating surveys with spatially varying detectability
text:
The covariate surface
The raster is read at the animals’ x and y coordinates, so it must be in the same CRS as the region. We project the canopy cover layer and write it to a GeoTIFF. A file path is better than an in-memory raster for parallel runs, because each worker then reads the file itself instead of receiving a copy of the raster.

canopy <- rast(here("data", "RMNP", "lidar", "lidar_pabove2_zmax_30m.tif"))[[1]] |>
  project(paste0("EPSG:", LOCAL))
names(canopy) <- "pabove2"
canopy_file <- here("workflow", "outputs", "pabove2_local.tif")
writeRaster(canopy, canopy_file, overwrite = TRUE)

Animals outside the raster, here the 3.5% of the park without lidar data, get the raster mean, and dsims warns when this happens.

title: Simulating surveys with spatially varying detectability
text:
Detectability that depends on canopy
We use the fitted hazard-rate detection function for moose: the scale parameter at zero canopy cover (scale_moose), the shape parameter, and the canopy coefficient beta_pabove2. The name of the entry in cov.surface must match the name in cov.param.

detect_canopy <- make.detectability(
  key.function = "hr",
  scale.param = scale_moose,
  shape.param = shape,
  cov.param = list(pabove2 = beta_pabove2),
  cov.surface = list(pabove2 = canopy_file),
  truncation = TRUNCATION_M
)


plot(detect_canopy, pop_desc)







Figure 1: Detection function for simulated moose at the mean canopy cover of the raster (solid), and at the canopy values that bound 95% of the raster (dashed).





A single simulated survey shows the covariate at work. The canopy value at each detected animal is carried into the survey data, where the analysis can use it.

set.seed(2025)
sim_one <- make.simulation(reps = 1, design = design_full, population.description = pop_desc,
                           detectability = detect_canopy,
                           ds.analysis = make.ds.analysis(dfmodel = ~1, key = "hr", truncation = TRUNCATION_M))
survey <- run.survey(sim_one)
detections <- survey@dist.data[!is.na(survey@dist.data$object), ]
nrow(detections)

[1] 229



detections$canopy_class <- cut(detections$pabove2, c(-Inf, 20, 30, Inf),
                               labels = c("< 20%", "20-30%", "> 30%"))
ggplot(detections, aes(distance)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 25, boundary = 0) +
  facet_wrap(~canopy_class) +
  labs(x = "Distance (m)", y = "Detections") +
  theme_minimal()

title: Simulating surveys with spatially varying detectability
text:
Analyses
Each simulated survey is analysed in two ways. The first ignores canopy (~1) and relies on pooling robustness: the property that a detection function without covariates can still estimate density without bias when detectability varies between animals (Buckland et al. 2001). The second offers AIC a choice between ~1 and ~pabove2, as in the real analysis. Both use the hazard-rate key.

analysis_null <- make.ds.analysis(dfmodel = ~1, key = "hr", truncation = TRUNCATION_M)
analysis_canopy <- make.ds.analysis(dfmodel = list(~1, ~pabove2), key = c("hr", "hr"),
                                    truncation = TRUNCATION_M, criteria = "AIC")

For the subplot designs, the subplots are strata of the design but should be analysed together, like the grouped strata in the dsims article Grouped strata. group.strata maps every subplot to a single analysis stratum.

group_all <- data.frame(design.id = sub_region@strata.name, analysis.id = "subplots")
analysis_null_sub <- make.ds.analysis(dfmodel = ~1, key = "hr", truncation = TRUNCATION_M,
                                      group.strata = group_all)
analysis_canopy_sub <- make.ds.analysis(dfmodel = list(~1, ~pabove2), key = c("hr", "hr"),
                                        truncation = TRUNCATION_M, criteria = "AIC",
                                        group.strata = group_all)

title: Simulating surveys with spatially varying detectability
text:
Running the simulations
Six simulations combine the three designs with the two analyses, each with 100 repetitions. Every repetition generates a new population, a new set of transects and new detections, and fits the detection function. The simulations run in parallel and take several minutes each; for your own designs, start with 20 repetitions to check the setup.

REPS <- 100
set.seed(2025)
run <- function(design, pop, analysis) {
  sim <- make.simulation(reps = REPS, design = design, population.description = pop,
                         detectability = detect_canopy, ds.analysis = analysis)
  run.simulation(sim, run.parallel = TRUE)
}

scenarios <- data.frame(
  design = rep(c("whole park, systematic", "subplots, systematic", "subplots, zigzag"), each = 2),
  analysis = rep(c("~1", "AIC: ~1 or ~pabove2"), 3)
)
sims <- list(
  run(design_full, pop_desc, analysis_null),
  run(design_full, pop_desc, analysis_canopy),
  run(design_sys, pop_desc_sub, analysis_null_sub),
  run(design_sys, pop_desc_sub, analysis_canopy_sub),
  run(design_zz, pop_desc_sub, analysis_null_sub),
  run(design_zz, pop_desc_sub, analysis_canopy_sub)
)
saveRDS(list(scenarios = scenarios, sims = sims), here("workflow", "outputs", "simulations.rds"))

title: Simulating surveys with spatially varying detectability
text:
Results
We compare the designs on density, because the subplot designs estimate density within the subplots, not across the whole park. For each simulation we extract the true and mean estimated density (animals per km²), the bias, the root mean squared error relative to the true density (RRMSE), the proportion of 95% confidence intervals that contain the true value, and the mean coefficient of variation.

sim_metrics <- function(sim) {
  s <- summary(sim, description.summary = FALSE)
  D <- s@individuals$D
  D <- D[nrow(D), ] # the total, or the single analysis stratum
  data.frame(
    true_D = D$Truth * 1e6,
    mean_D = D$mean.Estimate * 1e6,
    bias_pct = D$percent.bias,
    rrmse = D$RMSE / D$Truth,
    ci_coverage = D$CI.coverage.prob,
    mean_cv = D$mean.se / D$mean.Estimate
  )
}
results <- cbind(scenarios, do.call(rbind, lapply(sims, sim_metrics)))

How often did AIC choose the canopy model? The Detection results record which candidate model was selected in each repetition.

whole park, systematic   subplots, systematic       subplots, zigzag 
                  0.83                   0.72                   0.73 


With 100 repetitions, the Monte Carlo standard error of the bias is about one percentage point: the standard deviation of the estimates divided by \(\sqrt{100}\). Differences in bias of a point or two are therefore not meaningful.

Bias. The bias ranges from -0.2% to 2.4%. That is small next to the CV of about 10% of a single survey, and no design or analysis stands out.
Ignoring canopy. Even when detectability depends on canopy, a detection function without covariates (~1) estimates density as well as one with it. This is pooling robustness at work: the detection function averages over the variation in detectability, and because each design samples canopy conditions in proportion to their extent in the area it estimates for, the average is the right one (Buckland et al. 2001). Pooling robustness does not protect estimates for parts of the area with different canopy, such as density in dense forest alone (Rexstad et al. 2023).
Including canopy. AIC chose the canopy model in 72–83% of repetitions. Including it changes neither the bias nor the RRMSE materially, so for the overall density it does not make the estimate more accurate.
Precision. The RRMSE ranges from 0.09 to 0.11. The subplot designs estimate density within the subplots about as precisely as the whole-park design estimates it for the park, with less effort.
Confidence intervals. Coverage ranges from 0.92 to 0.96. With 100 repetitions, coverage itself has a Monte Carlo standard error of about 0.02, so this is consistent with the nominal 95% for all designs.

The estimates from each repetition are stored in sim@results$individuals$D, an array of strata × statistics × repetitions. Its last two slices hold the mean and standard deviation across repetitions, and the last row is the total.

title: Simulating surveys with spatially varying detectability
text:
Discussion
For moose in Riding Mountain National Park, drone surveys confined to subplots sized for one flight estimate the density within the subplots as accurately as a design across the whole park. They do this with about 13% less transect, and the zigzag spends the largest share of flying time on effort (Survey designs with subplots). Canopy-dependent detectability, simulated here with the cov.surface argument, did not bias any design. Ignoring canopy in the analysis was also safe for the overall density.
Two caveats matter when using these results for planning:

The estimate is for the subplots, not the park. Here the subplots happen to have almost the same density as the park, but that is not guaranteed. To estimate abundance for the whole park from subplots, the survey data have to be modelled with a DSM, predicting from habitat covariates as in Fitting a density surface model.
The results are specific to this landscape. The effect of spatially varying detectability depends on how canopy is distributed and where the transects fall. In denser forest, or with subplots placed in unrepresentative habitat, the conclusions could change. Checking that is exactly what cov.surface makes possible.

title: From density surface model to simulation
text:
Simulation lets us test a survey design before flying it: we generate many populations of animals, survey each one with the design, analyse the simulated data and compare the estimates with the true values. The dsims package does this. It builds a simulation from a region, a population, a detection process, a survey design and an analysis. Its article Getting started introduces these components with an invented density surface made of hotspots.
For a realistic test, the simulated animals should be distributed like the real ones and detected like the real ones. In this article we turn the results of the analysis into the objects that dsims expects: the density surface models from Fitting a density surface model, the group sizes, and the detection function from Estimating the detection function. We do this for moose, deer and elk, the three species with enough sightings. The conversion from a DSM to a dsims density is not covered in the dsims documentation.


The simulation articles run on any operating system with the repetitions set as shown. If you are an advanced user who wants to run many different simulations, or many more repetitions, consider running them on Linux, or on Windows through the Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL). On Linux, R can start parallel workers by forking the running session, so they share its loaded packages and data instead of each starting a fresh R session and receiving its own copy, as on Windows. Parallel simulations therefore start faster and use less memory. Windows remains perfectly usable for following these articles, but it is not the platform of choice for heavy simulation work.

title: From density surface model to simulation
text:
Prerequisites

library(here)
library(dsims) # simulation (loads dssd for designs)
library(dsm)
library(Distance)
library(sf)
library(terra)
library(exactextractr)
library(ggplot2)

The simulation articles use forks of dsims and dssd (see Packages). This article runs with the CRAN versions as well, but Simulating spatially varying detectability and Simulating a multi-species survey need the dsims fork:
remotes::install_github(c("hambrecht/dssd", "hambrecht/dsims"))
We load the data and prediction grid from Adding covariates and building a prediction grid, the per-species DSMs from Fitting a density surface model, and the detection function from Estimating the detection function.

model_data <- readRDS(here("workflow", "outputs", "model_data.rds"))
list2env(model_data, envir = environment())

<environment: R_GlobalEnv>

dsm_species <- readRDS(here("workflow", "outputs", "dsm_models.rds"))$dsm_species
df_best <- readRDS(here("workflow", "outputs", "detection_function.rds"))

SIM_SPECIES <- c("Moose", "Deer", "Elk")

title: From density surface model to simulation
text:
Setting up the region
The region is the study area polygon. It must be in the same projected coordinate system as the data the DSMs were fitted to, because the density grid below takes its x and y coordinates from the region. With units = "m", all lengths are in metres and areas in square metres.

region <- make.region(region.name = "RMNP", shape = area, units = "m")
region@area / 1e6 # km2

From density surface model to density grid

The density grid
make.density() lays a grid over the region. We use the same 500 m spacing as the prediction grid in the DSM articles.

density <- make.density(region = region, x.space = CELL_SIZE_M)
cells <- density@density.surface[[1]]

The grid is stored in the density.surface slot, one sf table per stratum. Each row is a grid cell with its centre (x, y) and a density column that is 1 everywhere by default. The cells along the boundary are clipped to the region, so not every cell covers the full 500 × 500 m.

cells$area <- as.numeric(st_area(cells))
summary(cells$area)

1.807e+00 2.500e+05 2.500e+05 2.425e+05 2.500e+05 2.500e+05 




Covariates for the grid
A habitat DSM needs its covariates to make a prediction, so we extract them for each cell of the dsims grid, exactly as we did for the prediction grid. A few cells lie outside the lidar coverage. We give them the median value from the surveyed segments, as the original RMNP analysis did for segments with missing values.

lidar <- rast(here("data", "RMNP", "lidar", "lidar_pabove2_zmax_10m.tif"))
names(lidar) <- c("pabove2", "zmax")

cell_covs <- exact_extract(lidar, cells, fun = "mean", progress = FALSE)
names(cell_covs) <- names(lidar)
sum(!complete.cases(cell_covs))

[1] 390

for (v in names(cell_covs)) cell_covs[[v]][is.na(cell_covs[[v]])] <- median(segs[[v]])

newdata <- data.frame(x = cells$x, y = cells$y, cell_covs, area = cells$area)



Predicting a DSM onto the grid
predict() gives the expected number of animals in each cell. The offset is each cell’s own area; using the nominal cell size instead would overestimate abundance in the clipped cells along the boundary. dsims reads the density column as animals per unit area, here per square metre, so we divide by the cell area before writing the prediction into the grid.

dsm_to_density <- function(model, density, newdata) {
  N_cell <- predict(model, newdata, off.set = newdata$area)
  density@density.surface[[1]]$density <- as.numeric(N_cell) / newdata$area
  density
}

densities <- lapply(dsm_species[SIM_SPECIES], dsm_to_density, density = density, newdata = newdata)
N_animals <- sapply(densities, function(d) sum(d@density.surface[[1]]$density * newdata$area))
round(N_animals)

Moose  Deer   Elk 
  458   545   230 


This is the key step. Any model that predicts animals per cell can be converted this way: a DSM with habitat covariates, a spatial smooth, or a model fitted to a previous survey. make.density() can also take a fitted GAM through its fitted.model argument, as in the Getting started article. That only works for models of x and y alone, though; it cannot supply habitat covariates or a cell-specific offset.

maps <- do.call(rbind, lapply(SIM_SPECIES, function(s) {
  surf <- densities[[s]]@density.surface[[1]]
  st_sf(species = s, D = surf$density * 1e6, geometry = st_geometry(surf))
}))
ggplot(maps) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = D), colour = NA) +
  facet_wrap(~species, ncol = 1) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Animals / km²") +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 1: Density surfaces used for the simulations (animals per km²). Elk have an intercept-only model, so their density is uniform.





The uniform band along the eastern edge of the moose and deer maps is the area without lidar data, where every cell has the median covariate values and therefore the same density.

text:
Defining the population
The population description combines the density grid with the population size. We set the size to the DSM estimate and fix it (fixed.N = TRUE), so every simulated population has exactly that many moose, distributed in proportion to the density grid.

N_moose <- round(sum(N_cell))
pop_desc <- make.population.description(region = region, density = density,
                                        N = N_moose, fixed.N = TRUE)
N_moose

[1] 447


The total differs slightly from the estimate in Estimating abundance because the dsims region includes the cells outside the lidar coverage, which the prediction grid dropped.

title: From density surface model to simulation
text:
Defining detectability
The detection process comes from the fitted detection function: a hazard-rate key whose scale depends on species and canopy cover. Distance reports the scale coefficients on the log scale, with moose as the reference level; make.detectability() expects the scale and shape on the natural scale. The scale for each species at zero canopy cover is therefore \(\exp(\beta_0 + \beta_\text{species})\).

coefs <- summary(df_best)$ds$coeff
beta <- setNames(coefs$key.scale$estimate, rownames(coefs$key.scale))
scale_species <- exp(beta["(Intercept)"] + c(Moose = 0, beta[paste0("Species", SIM_SPECIES[-1])]))
names(scale_species) <- SIM_SPECIES
shape <- exp(coefs$key.shape["(Intercept)", "estimate"])
beta_pabove2 <- beta[["pabove2"]]
round(c(scale_species, shape = shape, beta_pabove2 = beta_pabove2), 4)

       Moose         Deer          Elk        shape beta_pabove2 
    258.6623     144.5871     223.8232       2.2537      -0.0101 


These are the parameters of the pooled detection function in the RMNP analysis: hazard-rate, with species and lidar canopy cover as covariates.
For the design comparison in the next article we use a single, constant detection function for moose, evaluated at the median canopy cover of the moose sightings. The later articles use the canopy covariate in full.

pabove2_median <- median(dist$pabove2[dist$Species == "Moose"])
detect_constant <- make.detectability(
  key.function = "hr",
  scale.param = scale_species[["Moose"]] * exp(beta_pabove2 * pabove2_median),
  shape.param = shape,
  truncation = TRUNCATION_M
)


plot(detect_constant, pop_descs$Moose)







Figure 2: Moose detection function used in the design comparison, at the median canopy cover of moose sightings.

Checking the population
Generating one population and plotting it is a quick visual check that groups are placed where the DSM predicts them.

pop <- generate.population(pop_descs$Moose, detect_constant, region)
plot(pop, region)

       N_animals = N_animals, group_size = group_size, detect_constant = detect_constant,

title: From density surface model to simulation
text: References

title: Fitting a density surface model
text:
A density surface model (DSM) is a two-stage model (Miller et al. 2013). The detection function corrects each segment’s count for the animals that were missed. A generalized additive model (GAM) then relates the corrected counts to covariates, so that density can be predicted anywhere the covariates are known. In this article we fit DSMs for moose in Riding Mountain National Park, check them, and assess whether predicting over the whole park is an extrapolation.
We follow the habitat-based approach of Roberts et al. (2016). Density is modelled from habitat covariates only, without a spatial smooth of the coordinates, so the model describes why moose are where they are rather than just where they were seen. Each species gets its own model. For comparison we also fit a purely spatial model, as in the dsm example A simple DSM analysis: Gulf of Mexico dolphins.

The observation table holds all species. For the moose model we keep only moose sightings, while the detection function, fitted to all species, still provides each sighting’s detection probability.

Almost 98% of segments have no moose. This is typical of aerial surveys and it shapes the choice of response distribution.

title: Fitting a density surface model
text:
Response and response distribution
Because the detection function includes covariates, each sighting has its own detection probability. The response is therefore abundance.est: the count in each segment divided by the detection probabilities of its sightings (a Horvitz–Thompson estimate). This is non-negative and continuous, with a large mass of exact zeros.
The Tweedie distribution (tw()) models exactly this: it has a point mass at zero and a continuous density above zero, with its power parameter estimated from the data. The alternative, quasi-Poisson, is a mean–variance relationship for integer counts rather than a full distribution, and it has no likelihood, so it cannot be compared by AIC. Tweedie was also the choice of Roberts et al. (2016) for zero-inflated line-transect data.
All models are fitted by REML with gamma = 1.4, which penalises wiggliness a little more than the default and guards against overfitting (Wood 2017).

text:
A spatial model
The simplest DSM smooths abundance over the coordinates of the segment centroids. It shows where moose were seen but explains nothing about why.

title: Fitting a density surface model
text:
Habitat models
We have two candidate habitat covariates: canopy cover (pabove2) and canopy height (zmax). Each enters as a thin-plate shrinkage smooth (bs = "ts") with k = 5, which caps each smooth at about four degrees of freedom. This keeps the fitted responses simple enough to interpret and to trust outside the exact conditions sampled. The shrinkage basis can shrink a smooth all the way to zero, so an unhelpful covariate effectively drops out.

dsm_p2 <- dsm(abundance.est ~ s(pabove2, bs = "ts", k = 5), df_best, segs, obs_moose,
              family = tw(), gamma = 1.4, method = "REML")
dsm_zmax <- dsm(abundance.est ~ s(zmax, bs = "ts", k = 5), df_best, segs, obs_moose,
                family = tw(), gamma = 1.4, method = "REML")
dsm_both <- dsm(abundance.est ~ s(pabove2, bs = "ts", k = 5) + s(zmax, bs = "ts", k = 5),
                df_best, segs, obs_moose,
                family = tw(), gamma = 1.4, method = "REML")


Concurvity
Canopy cover and canopy height both describe the structure of the forest, so they are related. In a GAM this is called concurvity, the non-linear version of collinearity. When two smooths are concurve, their individual shapes become unstable and their uncertainty is inflated, even if the combined prediction looks reasonable. Values close to 1 are a warning sign.

cor(segs$pabove2, segs$zmax)

[1] 0.7133894

para       1.000000e+00 6.274191e-32 3.345868e-33
s(pabove2) 9.880595e-31 1.000000e+00 5.712405e-01
s(zmax)    5.875180e-32 4.605427e-01 1.000000e+00


Here the concurvity is moderate (about 0.5). With the full set of lidar metrics, however, cover and height metrics reached concurvity of 0.98 in the RMNP analysis, so every cover metric was paired with a height metric in a banned list, and only one of the two families may enter a model. We keep that rule here. Following Roberts et al. (2016), we choose the covariate that explains more deviance on its own, and then retain it only if its smooth is significant (\(p \le 0.05\)) and not shrunk away (effective degrees of freedom, EDF, of at least 0.85).

  model = c("s(pabove2)", "s(zmax)"),
  dev_expl = c(summary(dsm_p2)$dev.expl, summary(dsm_zmax)$dev.expl),

Extrapolation
A DSM is only reliable where the prediction grid resembles the conditions that were surveyed. dsmextra identifies prediction cells whose covariate values lie outside the range of the segments (univariate extrapolation) or in combinations not seen in the segments (combinatorial extrapolation) (Bouchet et al. 2020).

title: Fitting a density surface model
text:
Other species
The same procedure applies to the other species. Following Roberts et al. (2016), the model’s complexity depends on how often a species was seen. Species with at least 40 sightings get a habitat model chosen as above. Species with fewer than 20 get an intercept-only model: this estimates the average density across the study area without trying to map it.

fit_species <- function(species, covariates = c("pabove2", "zmax")) {
  obs_sp <- obs[obs$Species == species, ]
  fit <- function(rhs) {
    dsm(as.formula(paste("abundance.est ~", rhs)), df_best, segs, obs_sp,
        family = tw(), gamma = 1.4, method = "REML")
  }
  if (nrow(obs_sp) < 20) return(fit("1"))

  # One covariate (they are concurve): the one with most deviance explained
  singles <- lapply(covariates, function(v) fit(sprintf("s(%s, bs = 'ts', k = 5)", v)))
  best <- singles[[which.max(sapply(singles, function(m) summary(m)$dev.expl))]]

  # Keep it only if significant and not shrunk away
  st <- summary(best)$s.table
  if (st[1, "p-value"] <= 0.05 && st[1, "edf"] >= 0.85) best else fit("1")
}

species_list <- c("Moose", "Deer", "Elk", "Bison", "Wolf")
dsm_species <- lapply(setNames(species_list, species_list), fit_species)
sapply(dsm_species, function(m) deparse(formula(m)))

Canopy height is retained for moose and deer. For elk neither canopy metric meets the selection criteria, so elk also get an intercept-only model. Covariates other than the two used here would likely help. In the full RMNP analysis, which also considered elevation and distance to forest edge, elevation was the strongest predictor for all three species.

title: Adding covariates and building a prediction grid
text:
Density surface models explain variation in counts along the transects using spatial and environmental covariates, and then predict density over the whole study area from the same covariates. Covariates therefore have to be available in three places: at each sighting (to model detectability), for each segment (to fit the density surface model), and for each cell of a prediction grid (to predict from it). The dsm examples skip this step because their data ship with covariates already attached. Here we extract them from raster layers.
We use two canopy metrics derived from airborne lidar over Riding Mountain National Park, both at 10 m resolution:

pabove2: the percentage of lidar returns above 2 m, a measure of canopy cover. Dense cover may hide animals from observers and also shapes where moose feed and shelter.
zmax: the maximum canopy height (m), which separates open areas, shrubs, young regenerating stands and mature forest.

Any raster layer can be used in the same way. The only requirements are that it covers the whole study area and that it describes something plausibly linked to detectability or density.

Covariate rasters
Both metrics are stored as the two layers of a single GeoTIFF, as whole numbers (percent and metres) to keep the file small. The raster is already in the workflow CRS; if yours is not, reproject it once with terra::project() before starting, rather than in every script.

lidar <- rast(here("data", "RMNP", "lidar", "lidar_pabove2_zmax_10m.tif"))

text:
Detection covariates at sightings
Vegetation near an animal may hide it from observers, so both metrics at each sighting location are candidate covariates for the detection function. They are extracted at the sighting points.

pts <- vect(dist, geom = c("X", "Y"), crs = paste0("EPSG:", LOCAL))
dist <- cbind(dist, extract(lidar, pts, ID = FALSE))

text:
Segment covariates
For segments we summarise each covariate over the strip actually searched: the segment buffered by the truncation distance. exact_extract() weights each raster cell by the fraction of it inside the strip, and we take the mean.

strips <- st_buffer(segs, dist = TRUNCATION_M)
seg_means <- exact_extract(lidar, strips, fun = "mean", progress = FALSE)
names(seg_means) <- names(lidar)

segs <- segs |>
  bind_cols(seg_means) |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  as.data.frame()

One segment lies outside the lidar coverage. It has no sightings, so we can drop it; had it contained sightings, those would need to be dropped from dist and obs too.

segs <- segs[complete.cases(segs[, names(lidar)]), ]
stopifnot(all(obs$Sample.Label %in% segs$Sample.Label))

title: Adding covariates and building a prediction grid
text:
Prediction grid
The prediction grid covers the study area with square cells. Cells should not be much smaller than the segments: the model cannot resolve detail below the scale it was sampled at, and many small cells make variance estimation slow. We use 500 m cells, about the length of one segment.

CELL_SIZE_M <- 500

cells <- st_make_grid(area, cellsize = CELL_SIZE_M, what = "polygons")
centres <- st_centroid(cells)
inside <- lengths(st_intersects(centres, area)) > 0

pred <- st_sf(geometry = cells[inside])
xy <- st_coordinates(centres[inside])
pred$x <- xy[, 1]
pred$y <- xy[, 2]
pred$area <- CELL_SIZE_M^2
nrow(pred)

[1] 12485


The same covariates are then extracted for every cell.

pred_means <- exact_extract(lidar, pred, fun = "mean", progress = FALSE)
names(pred_means) <- names(lidar)
pred <- bind_cols(pred, pred_means)

pred <- pred[complete.cases(st_drop_geometry(pred)), ]
nrow(pred)

[1] 12214


Cells with missing covariate values fall outside the lidar coverage and are dropped: predicting there would mean predicting without data.

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = pred, aes(fill = pabove2), colour = NA) +
  geom_point(data = segs, aes(x, y), size = 0.1, colour = "white") +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "pabove2 (%)") +
  theme_minimal()

title: R workflow: density surface models for aerial ungulate surveys
text:
This series of articles walks through a complete distance sampling analysis of an aerial survey in R: from raw sightings and flight lines to maps of density and estimates of abundance with their uncertainty. The results are then used to simulate and compare designs for future drone surveys. It uses real data from a 2025 thermal-drone survey of moose, elk, deer, bison and wolves in Riding Mountain National Park, Manitoba.
The articles are written in the same style as the dsm and dsims package articles on distancesampling.org, and link to them where they cover the general method. They add the steps those examples leave out: turning flight tracks into segments, extracting covariates from raster layers, building a prediction grid, and fitting species-specific models to a multi-species survey following Roberts et al. (2016).

Adding covariates and building a prediction grid
Extracts lidar canopy cover and height at sightings, over segment strips and over a 500 m prediction grid
terra, exactextractr


Estimating the detection function
Fits half-normal and hazard-rate detection functions with species and canopy covariates and selects one by AIC
Distance


Fitting a density surface model
Fits habitat and spatial DSMs per species, checks them and assesses extrapolation
dsm, dsmextra


Estimating abundance and its uncertainty
Predicts density, estimates variance, maps uncertainty and tabulates abundance for all species
dsm


From density surface model to simulation
Converts the moose DSM and detection function into the region, density, population and detectability objects of dsims
dsims


Survey designs with subplots
Generates subplots sized for one drone flight, places systematic and zigzag transects inside them, and compares coverage and effort with a design across the whole park
dsims, dssd


Simulating surveys with spatially varying detectability
Simulates surveys in which detectability depends on canopy cover at each animal, and compares designs and analyses
dsims (fork)



The first five articles are the core analysis. The last three use its results to test survey designs by simulation and can be skipped if you only need estimates from your own survey.
Each article ends by saving its results to workflow/outputs/, and the next one starts by loading them. You can therefore start at any article, as long as the files from the previous step exist.
All the code of the five core articles is also available as a single script, rmnp_workflow.R. It includes the data check functions, and it is the easiest starting point for analysing your own survey: replace the file names and column names in the first section, run the checks, and work through the script. The simulation articles are kept separate, because they are only needed when planning a new survey.

title: When Is a Quadcopter the Right Tool for Wildlife Surveys?
text:
Authors: Leonard Hambrecht, Nicholas C. Coops, Gordon Stenhouse, Philip DeWitt, Jason Airst
Keywords: Distance sampling, thermal, UAV, UAS, density, population estimate, detection function, survey design

title: When Is a Quadcopter the Right Tool for Wildlife Surveys?
text:
Overview
Quadcopters — compact, off-the-shelf multirotor drones — have become widely used for wildlife monitoring. They are inexpensive, easy to deploy in rugged terrain, and capable of carrying thermal cameras that detect animals day or night. But for all their appeal, a critical question has remained unanswered: at what animal density do they actually produce reliable population estimates, and which flight design gets you there most efficiently?
This study addresses that gap through a systematic simulation study, evaluating five quadcopter survey designs across ten wildlife density levels in a controlled 10 × 10 km landscape. The goal is to give wildlife managers practical, evidence-based guidelines for deciding when — and how — to use a quadcopter for population surveys.

title: When Is a Quadcopter the Right Tool for Wildlife Surveys?
text:
Study Design
We built an artificial density surface model representing a 10 × 10 km study area with realistic spatial heterogeneity — clustered hotspots and low-use zones — similar to how large mammals actually distribute themselves across a landscape. We simulated wildlife populations ranging from 50 to 900 individuals per 1,000 km², covering the density ranges typical of deer, moose, elephants, and large carnivores.
The area was divided into 2 × 2 km sample blocks, representing one day of surveying under extended line-of-sight conditions. We tested configurations of 4, 9, 16, and 25 blocks and compared five flight designs:







Design
Description




65% overlap
Standard orthomosaic mapping overlap


10% overlap
Minimum supported by flight-planning software


0% overlap
Non-overlapping strip transects


200 m spacing
Fixed wide spacing, manually planned


Gimbal (line transect)
Camera pans left-right; half-normal detection function, 155 m half-width



Each of the 200 unique simulation scenarios was replicated 999 times. Performance was evaluated using bias, coefficient of variation (CV ≤ 0.15 as the precision threshold), and root mean square deviation (RMSE).

title: When Is a Quadcopter the Right Tool for Wildlife Surveys?
text:
Key Findings
The 65% overlap design is the most precise — but comes at a steep cost. This design reliably met the CV threshold across all densities and block configurations, but required roughly eleven times more survey effort than the gimbal design. It also introduced a real risk of double-counting animals that moved between passes, a problem that must be carefully managed in the field.
The 10% and 0% overlap designs hit a sweet spot for moderate-density populations. Above 400 individuals per 1,000 km², these designs achieved acceptable precision when 9–16 sample blocks were surveyed, with substantially less effort than the 65% design. They are the recommended choice for species in that density range.
The 200 m spacing design underperforms across the board. It consistently overestimated population size, failed to meet the precision threshold at any density, and produced insufficient detections at low densities. It is not recommended for population estimation.
The gimbal line-transect design requires high effort to work. Despite being the most effort-efficient per km flown, the gimbal design needed all 25 sample blocks to meet the CV threshold, and only did so at the highest tested density. For quadcopters operating within their typical 2 × 2 km range, the strip transect designs are more practical.
Survey effort and precision are tightly linked. Designs requiring 300–500 km of on-transect effort produced reliable estimates above ~800 individuals per 1,000 km²; efforts above 800 km extended reliability down to ~500 individuals per 1,000 km². At low densities, high overlap may be necessary — but introduces double-counting risks that require careful image review.

title: When Is a Quadcopter the Right Tool for Wildlife Surveys?
text:
Practical Recommendations
For densities above 400 individuals per 1,000 km²: Use 0% or 10% overlap strip transects with 9–16 sample blocks. This balances accuracy and effort without the double-counting risks of high overlap.
For densities below 400 individuals per 1,000 km²: Use 65% overlap with a census approach and carefully review images to remove double-counted individuals. Alternatively, reconsider whether a quadcopter is the right platform — low-density, large-area surveys may be better served by a fixed-wing drone.
For areas larger than 10 × 10 km: Fixed-wing drones combined with line-transect distance sampling are a more efficient and rigorous option. Quadcopters are well-matched to small, accessible study areas where rugged terrain precludes fixed-wing operations.
Avoid the 200 m spacing design for population estimation — its systematic overestimation makes it unsuitable regardless of effort.

title: When Is a Quadcopter the Right Tool for Wildlife Surveys?
text:
Why This Matters
As drone technology becomes more accessible, the temptation to use a quadcopter for everything grows. This study provides a clear-eyed assessment of where quadcopters genuinely excel (moderate-to-high density, small study areas, rugged terrain) and where their limitations become a liability (large areas, low-density species, extensive coverage requirements). By matching the tool to the task, wildlife managers can get rigorous, cost-effective population estimates — and avoid the pitfall of precise-sounding numbers that are quietly biased.

Hambrecht, L., Coops, N. C., Stenhouse, G., DeWitt, P., & Airst, J. When is a quadcopter the right tool for wildlife surveys? Assessing quadcopter applications to monitor populations. Manuscript in preparation.

Use zigzag transects for fixed-wing drones. They achieved up to 96.6% of flight time on-transect, compared to 80.5% for the helicopter’s segmented grid design. (Multi-platform Simulations)

Avoid nadir-only camera configurations. A straight-down camera assumes uniform detection within a narrow strip and significantly overestimates density. (Multi-platform Simulations)
Equip quadcopters with a gimbal or dual-camera setup when a wider, angled field of view is needed — this brings quadcopter estimates much closer to fixed-wing accuracy. (Multi-platform Simulations)
Use thermal infrared sensors for nighttime or low-visibility surveys. Thermal imagery mitigates visual occlusion and enables detection outside daylight hours. (Deep Learning)

title: Optimizing Wildlife Survey Design: Simulating Drone and Helicopter Surveys for Moose
text:
Authors: Leonard Hambrecht, Nicholas C. Coops, Gordon Stenhouse
Keywords: Alces alces, density estimation, detection function, distance sampling, survey design, thermal, UAV, UAS

title: Optimizing Wildlife Survey Design: Simulating Drone and Helicopter Surveys for Moose
text:
Overview
Accurate moose population estimates are essential for wildlife management across Canada’s vast boreal landscapes, but conventional helicopter surveys come with significant costs: high expense, safety risks to observers, and increasing CO₂ emissions. Drone technology offers a compelling alternative — but how well does it actually perform?
This study uses a simulation-based framework to rigorously compare fixed-wing drones, quadcopters, and conventional helicopters for estimating moose (Alces alces) populations using line-transect distance sampling. Rather than running costly field trials across multiple designs, we simulated thousands of surveys using real moose population data from five Wildlife Management Units (WMUs) in Alberta, Canada — ranging from 2,132 to 12,034 km² — and tested how different platforms, camera configurations, and transect designs affect accuracy and efficiency.

title: Optimizing Wildlife Survey Design: Simulating Drone and Helicopter Surveys for Moose
text:
Study Area
The five WMUs are located north of Edmonton in Alberta’s boreal mixedwood forest. Moose densities varied from 0.085 to 0.442 moose/km², representing the low-density conditions typical of many large mammal surveys. These existing Government of Alberta helicopter survey data provided a realistic baseline for calibrating and comparing the simulations.

title: Optimizing Wildlife Survey Design: Simulating Drone and Helicopter Surveys for Moose
text:
What We Tested
We compared three aerial platforms across multiple survey designs:

Helicopter (baseline): segmented grid design with experienced human observers
Fixed-wing drone: systematic and zigzag transect designs
Quadcopter: systematic subplot design with two camera options — nadir (straight down) and gimbal (angled sweep)

Camera configuration was a key variable. We modeled three detection functions:

Nadir (straight-down camera): narrow 40 m strip half-width, uniform detection assumed
Two-camera / Gimbal: wider effective detection area, half-normal detection function — comparable to how biologists visually scan from a helicopter

Simulations varied moose density at 100%, 75%, 50%, and 25% of observed levels to test performance under increasingly challenging low-density conditions.

title: Optimizing Wildlife Survey Design: Simulating Drone and Helicopter Surveys for Moose
text:
Results



Figure 5. Mean estimated density for each simulation by WMU.





Figure 6. Summary statistics of the estimated density for each simulation, averaged across all WMUs. The summary statistics include the relative mean density (A), bias (B), relative RMSE (C), proportion of times the 95% confidence interval contained the true density (D), mean standard error (E), coefficient of variation (F), mean encounter rate (G), and mean standard error of the encounter rate (H).





Figure 7. Comparison of mean estimated density across different survey designs with varying input density levels (1x, 0.75x, 0.5x, 0.25x). The input densities are indicated by the dashed lines.

title: Optimizing Wildlife Survey Design: Simulating Drone and Helicopter Surveys for Moose
text:
Key Findings
Helicopters remain robust but tend to underestimate. The conventional segmented grid design achieved the highest survey coverage and performed well at low densities, but it systematically underestimated moose density — likely due to observer fatigue and imperfect detection near the transect line.
Fixed-wing drones are the most accurate alternative. Across all five WMUs and all density scenarios, fixed-wing drones using systematic or zigzag transects produced the most accurate density estimates. Even at low moose densities, the fixed-wing platform tracked the true density closely. The zigzag design was particularly efficient, spending up to 96.6% of flight time on-transect — compared to 80.5% for the helicopter.
Quadcopters with nadir cameras significantly overestimate density. Because the nadir configuration assumes perfect, uniform detection within a narrow 40 m strip, it severely overestimates moose numbers. With an average survey coverage of less than 10% of the study area, the quadcopter nadir design is poorly suited for low-density, large-area surveys.
Quadcopters improve substantially with a gimbal camera. When equipped with a gimbal that mimics the wider scanning angle of a helicopter observer, quadcopter estimates become much more comparable to fixed-wing results. However, coverage limitations persist — quadcopters simply cannot cover the same ground per unit time as a fixed-wing drone.
Efficiency matters. The zigzag fixed-wing design achieved the highest on-transect proportion (96.6%), minimizing time and fuel spent repositioning between transect lines. The helicopter design, despite its high coverage, spent nearly 20% of flight time off-transect transitioning between segments.

title: Optimizing Wildlife Survey Design: Simulating Drone and Helicopter Surveys for Moose
text:
Recommendations

Use fixed-wing drones as the primary alternative to helicopters for large-area, low-density moose surveys. They deliver accurate estimates with comparable efficiency.
Avoid nadir-only quadcopter configurations for population estimation — the narrow detection strip leads to severe overestimation.
Equip quadcopters with a gimbal or dual-camera setup if they must be used, substantially improving accuracy while acknowledging remaining coverage constraints.
Apply zigzag transect designs for fixed-wing platforms to maximize on-transect efficiency.

title: Optimizing Wildlife Survey Design: Simulating Drone and Helicopter Surveys for Moose
text:
Looking Ahead
These simulation results provide strong evidence that drone-based surveys can match or exceed helicopter performance under the right conditions. However, real-world factors — canopy cover, snow conditions, temperature, and regulatory airspace restrictions — will influence operational outcomes. This work sets the stage for field validation and practical deployment guidelines for drone-based moose monitoring across Canada’s boreal forest.

Hambrecht, L., Coops, N. C., & Stenhouse, G. Optimizing wildlife survey design: Simulating drone and helicopter surveys for moose detection and population estimation. Manuscript in preparation.

title: Deep Learning
text:
Author: Hiroto Goto, Nicholas C. Coops
Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) offer a promising alternative to conventional survey methods and can be equipped with thermal infrared sensors to mitigate visual occlusion and enable nighttime imaging. However, the large data volume generated from drone flights presents a significant bottleneck as manual review can be time-consuming, inefficient, and error prone. Recent advancements in deep learning have revolutionized the ability for automated wildlife detection from drone imagery using convolutional neural networks (CNNs). This study develops and validates a deep learning pipeline to automate the detection and classification of terrestrial mammals, including moose, across Canada’s forested boreal landscapes. Thermal footage was collected using a manually piloted fixed-wing UAV, and a multi-stage deep learning framework was implemented to identify candidate hotspots followed by species confirmation. The results demonstrate the feasibility of combining UAV thermal surveys with deep learning for scalable multi-species monitoring under challenging environmental conditions.

title: Formatting aerial survey data for density surface models
text:
This article is the first step of the R workflow for analysing aerial surveys of moose and other ungulates with distance sampling. We take the raw survey data, a table of sightings and a set of flight lines, and turn them into the three tables that Distance and dsm expect: detection data, segment data and observation data. The general principles are covered in the dsm article Data formatting for density surface models; here we apply them to a real thermal-drone survey.
The example data come from an aerial ungulate survey of Riding Mountain National Park (RMNP), Manitoba, in February 2025. The survey was flown by a fixed-wing drone (Superwake SW-117) carrying a gimbal-mounted thermal and RGB camera, along north–south transects spaced 600 m apart (1.6 km in places). Video was recorded continuously. For each detection the aircraft circled the group to count and identify the animals, and the group’s position was obtained by projecting the camera’s view onto a digital elevation model. Moose, elk, white-tailed deer, bison and wolves were recorded.

title: Formatting aerial survey data for density surface models
text:
Prerequisites
We need the following packages:

library(here)    # file paths relative to the project root
library(sf)      # vector spatial data
library(dplyr)   # data manipulation
library(units)   # unit-aware lengths
library(ggplot2) # plotting

The example data can be downloaded as rmnp_example_data.zip (36 MB). The following chunk downloads and unzips it into data/RMNP/ if it is not there yet, so you can follow along from an empty project folder.

if (!file.exists(here("data", "RMNP", "RMNPsightings.csv"))) {
  dir.create(here("data"), showWarnings = FALSE)
  zip_file <- here("data", "rmnp_example_data.zip")
  if (!file.exists(zip_file)) {
    download.file("https://hambrecht.github.io/mri/data/rmnp_example_data.zip",
                  zip_file, mode = "wb")
  }
  unzip(zip_file, exdir = here("data"))
}

If you use your own data, the minimum requirements are a table of sightings with coordinates, species and group size, and the flight lines flown on effort as a line layer.
All spatial operations happen in a projected coordinate reference system (CRS) so that distances and lengths are in metres. We use NAD83(CSRS) / Canada Atlas Lambert (EPSG:3979), which works across Canada; a local UTM zone is equally good. We define it once and use it everywhere.

LOCAL <- 3979  # projected CRS (metres) used throughout the workflow
GLOBAL <- 4326 # WGS84 longitude/latitude, as recorded in the field

title: Formatting aerial survey data for density surface models
text:
Overview
For a line-transect density surface model we need to build:

Detection data (dist): one row per sighting within the truncation distance, with the perpendicular distance, the group size, a unique object ID and any covariates that might affect detectability. This is what the detection function is fitted to.
Segment data (segs): one row per segment of transect, with a unique Sample.Label, the segment length Effort, the centroid coordinates x, y and any habitat covariates.
Observation data (obs): a lookup table linking each object to the Sample.Label of the segment it was seen from, along with size and distance.

The tables are linked by object (detection ↔︎ observation) and Sample.Label (observation ↔︎ segment).

title: Formatting aerial survey data for density surface models
text:
The survey data
We read the raw files as they are: the sightings as a CSV file with latitude and longitude in WGS84, the flight lines flown on effort, the study area boundary, and the covariate rasters used later.

sightings_raw <- read.csv(here("data", "RMNP", "RMNPsightings.csv"))
transects_raw <- st_read(here("data", "RMNP", "SimpliedFlightTrack.shp"), quiet = TRUE)
area_raw <- st_read(here("data", "RMNP", "RMNPArea.shp"), quiet = TRUE)
lidar <- terra::rast(here("data", "RMNP", "lidar", "lidar_pabove2_zmax_10m.tif"))
names(lidar) <- c("pabove2", "zmax")

Before analysis, the detections were quality-checked. Records with missing coordinates, records made while moving between transects or after dusk, and animals that could not be identified were removed; the file contains the 357 records that remained. We keep the five target species.

SPECIES_KEEP <- c("Moose", "Elk", "Deer", "Wolf", "Bison")
sightings_raw <- filter(sightings_raw, Species %in% SPECIES_KEEP)

title: Formatting aerial survey data for density surface models
text:
Checking the data
Most problems in a distance sampling analysis come from the input data. Examples are coordinates in the wrong system, group sizes stored as text, flight lines that are polygons, or sightings far from any line. These rarely cause an error; instead they quietly give wrong distances or wrong effort. check_survey_data() tests the raw inputs before any processing. It is defined in workflow/R/check_survey_data.R, shown in full at the end of this article.

source(here("workflow", "R", "check_survey_data.R"))

We pass the sightings (with the names of their species, group size and coordinate columns), the flight lines, the study area, the projected CRS we want to work in and, optionally, the covariate rasters. Each row of the result is one check, with the status PASS, WARN (worth a look), FAIL (must be fixed) or INFO. By default the function stops if any check fails; here we set stop_on_fail = FALSE to see the whole table.

checks <- check_survey_data(
  sightings_raw, transects_raw, area_raw, crs = LOCAL,
  species = "Species", size = "size", coords = c("Longitude", "Latitude"),
  covariates = lidar, stop_on_fail = FALSE
)

Perpendicular distances
The distance from each sighting to the nearest flight line is its perpendicular distance.

Truncation
Sightings far from the line carry little information about the shape of the detection function and can make fitting harder. A common rule is to discard the furthest 5% of distances (Buckland et al. 2001). We compute the truncation distance once here and reuse it in every later step, so the segment strip width, the detection function and the density surface model all agree.

text:
Appendix: the check functions

The two check functions, from workflow/R/check_survey_data.R. Copy the file into your own project and source() it. The tests in workflow/R/test-check_survey_data.R show each check catching the problem it is meant to catch.

# Compatibility checks for distance sampling / density surface model data.
#
# check_survey_data(): raw inputs (sightings, transects, study area, rasters)
#                      before any processing.
# check_dsm_data():    the formatted detection, segment, observation and
#                      prediction tables before fitting ds() and dsm().
#
# Both return a data.frame with one row per check (status PASS, WARN, FAIL or
# INFO), print it, and stop if any check FAILs (unless stop_on_fail = FALSE).

library(sf)

# Collects check results; `record(check, ok, detail)` adds a row.
new_checklist <- function() {
  rows <- list()
  record <- function(check, ok, detail = "", level = "FAIL") {
    status <- if (isTRUE(ok)) "PASS" else level
    if (status == "PASS") detail <- "" # details only where something needs attention
    rows[[length(rows) + 1]] <<- data.frame(check = check, status = status, detail = detail)
    invisible(isTRUE(ok))
  }
  info <- function(check, detail) record(check, FALSE, detail, level = "INFO")
  result <- function(stop_on_fail) {
    out <- do.call(rbind, rows)
    cat(sprintf("%-4s  %s%s\n", out$status, out$check,
                ifelse(out$detail == "", "", paste0(": ", out$detail))), sep = "")
    n_fail <- sum(out$status == "FAIL")
    if (stop_on_fail && n_fail > 0) {
      stop(n_fail, " check(s) failed; see the table above.", call. = FALSE)
    }
    invisible(out)
  }
  list(record = record, info = info, result = result)
}

check_survey_data <- function(sightings, transects, area, crs,
                              species = "Species", size = "size",
                              coords = c("Longitude", "Latitude"), coords_crs = 4326,
                              covariates = NULL, stop_on_fail = TRUE) {
  cl <- new_checklist()
  rec <- cl$record

  # --- Sightings -------------------------------------------------------------
  rec("sightings: has rows", nrow(sightings) > 0, sprintf("%d rows", nrow(sightings)))
  needed <- c(species, size, if (!inherits(sightings, "sf")) coords)
  missing_cols <- setdiff(needed, names(sightings))
  if (!rec("sightings: required columns", length(missing_cols) == 0,
           if (length(missing_cols)) paste("missing:", paste(missing_cols, collapse = ", ")) else "")) {
    return(cl$result(stop_on_fail))
  }

  if (inherits(sightings, "sf")) {
    n_empty <- sum(st_is_empty(sightings))
    rec("sightings: no empty geometries", n_empty == 0, sprintf("%d empty", n_empty))
    rec("sightings: CRS defined", !is.na(st_crs(sightings)))
    pts <- sightings[!st_is_empty(sightings), ]
  } else {
    xy <- sightings[, coords]
    bad_xy <- !stats::complete.cases(xy)
    rec("sightings: coordinates present", !any(bad_xy), sprintf("%d rows without coordinates", sum(bad_xy)))
    keep <- !bad_xy
    if (identical(coords_crs, 4326)) {
      out_range <- !bad_xy & (abs(xy[[1]]) > 180 | abs(xy[[2]]) > 90)
      rec("sightings: longitude/latitude in range", !any(out_range),
          sprintf("%d rows out of range (are longitude and latitude swapped or projected?)", sum(out_range)))
      keep <- keep & !out_range
    }
    if (!any(keep)) return(cl$result(stop_on_fail))
    pts <- st_as_sf(sightings[keep, ], coords = coords, crs = coords_crs, remove = FALSE)
  }
  if (nrow(pts) == 0) return(cl$result(stop_on_fail))

  sz <- sightings[[size]]
  rec("sightings: group size numeric", is.numeric(sz), class(sz)[1])
  if (is.numeric(sz)) {
    rec("sightings: group size present", !anyNA(sz), sprintf("%d missing", sum(is.na(sz))))
    rec("sightings: group size > 0", all(sz > 0, na.rm = TRUE), sprintf("%d <= 0", sum(sz <= 0, na.rm = TRUE)))
    rec("sightings: group size whole numbers", all(sz == round(sz), na.rm = TRUE),
        sprintf("%d non-integer", sum(sz != round(sz), na.rm = TRUE)), level = "WARN")
  }

  sp <- as.character(sightings[[species]])
  n_nosp <- sum(is.na(sp) | trimws(sp) == "")
  rec("sightings: species recorded", n_nosp == 0, sprintf("%d without species", n_nosp), level = "WARN")
  counts <- sort(table(sp[!is.na(sp) & trimws(sp) != ""]), decreasing = TRUE)
  cl$info("sightings: per species", paste(names(counts), counts, sep = " = ", collapse = ", "))

  dup <- duplicated(data.frame(pts[[species]], round(st_coordinates(pts), 6)))
  rec("sightings: no duplicate records", !any(dup),
      sprintf("%d with the same species and location", sum(dup)), level = "WARN")

  # --- Transects and study area ---------------------------------------------
  line_types <- c("LINESTRING", "MULTILINESTRING")
  rec("transects: sf line layer",
      inherits(transects, "sf") && all(st_geometry_type(transects) %in% line_types),
      if (inherits(transects, "sf")) paste(unique(st_geometry_type(transects)), collapse = ", ") else class(transects)[1])
  rec("area: sf polygon layer",
      inherits(area, c("sf", "sfc")) && all(st_geometry_type(area) %in% c("POLYGON", "MULTIPOLYGON")),
      if (inherits(area, c("sf", "sfc"))) paste(unique(st_geometry_type(area)), collapse = ", ") else class(area)[1])
  if (!inherits(transects, "sf") || !inherits(area, c("sf", "sfc"))) return(cl$result(stop_on_fail))

  rec("transects: CRS defined", !is.na(st_crs(transects)))
  rec("area: CRS defined", !is.na(st_crs(area)))
  rec("transects: valid geometries", all(st_is_valid(transects)), sprintf("%d invalid", sum(!st_is_valid(transects))))
  rec("area: valid geometry", all(st_is_valid(area)), "fix with sf::st_make_valid()")

  target <- st_crs(crs)
  projected_m <- !is.na(target) && !isTRUE(target$IsGeographic) && identical(target$units_gdal, "metre")
  rec("target CRS projected, in metres", projected_m,
      if (is.na(target)) "undefined" else paste0(target$Name, " (", target$units_gdal, ")"))
  if (!projected_m || is.na(st_crs(transects)) || is.na(st_crs(area)) || is.na(st_crs(pts))) {
    return(cl$result(stop_on_fail))
  }

  pts <- st_transform(pts, target)
  transects <- st_transform(transects, target)
  area <- st_union(st_transform(st_geometry(area), target))

  len <- as.numeric(st_length(transects))
  rec("transects: no zero-length lines", all(len > 0), sprintf("%d of %d", sum(len == 0), length(len)))
  cl$info("transects: total length", sprintf("%.1f km in %d features", sum(len) / 1000, length(len)))

  inside <- lengths(st_intersects(pts, area)) > 0
  rec("sightings: inside study area", all(inside), sprintf("%d outside", sum(!inside)), level = "WARN")
  len_in <- sum(as.numeric(st_length(st_intersection(st_geometry(transects), area))))
  rec("transects: inside study area", len_in / sum(len) >= 0.95,
      sprintf("%.1f%% of length inside", 100 * len_in / sum(len)), level = "WARN")

  d <- as.numeric(st_distance(pts, transects[st_nearest_feature(pts, transects), ], by_element = TRUE))
  q95 <- stats::quantile(d, 0.95)
  cl$info("distances: median / 95% / max (m)", sprintf("%.0f / %.0f / %.0f", stats::median(d), q95, max(d)))
  rec("distances: no extreme outliers", max(d) <= 3 * q95,
      sprintf("%d sightings > 3x the 95th percentile (off-effort, or wrong transect?)", sum(d > 3 * q95)),
      level = "WARN")

  # --- Covariate rasters (optional) -----------------------------------------
  if (!is.null(covariates)) {
    rec("covariates: CRS defined", terra::crs(covariates) != "")
    samp <- terra::vect(st_transform(st_sample(area, 2000), terra::crs(covariates)))
    na_area <- colMeans(is.na(terra::extract(covariates, samp, ID = FALSE)))
    rec("covariates: cover study area", all(na_area <= 0.05),
        paste(sprintf("%s %.1f%% missing", names(na_area), 100 * na_area), collapse = "; "), level = "WARN")
    na_pts <- colSums(is.na(terra::extract(covariates, terra::vect(st_transform(pts, terra::crs(covariates))), ID = FALSE)))
    rec("covariates: values at sightings", all(na_pts == 0),
        paste(sprintf("%s %d missing", names(na_pts), na_pts), collapse = "; "), level = "WARN")
  }

  cl$result(stop_on_fail)
}

check_dsm_data <- function(dist, segs, obs, pred = NULL, covariates = NULL,
                           truncation = NULL, stop_on_fail = TRUE) {
  cl <- new_checklist()
  rec <- cl$record

  required <- list(
    dist = c("object", "distance", "size"),
    segs = c("Sample.Label", "Effort", "x", "y"),
    obs = c("object", "Sample.Label", "size", "distance"),
    pred = c("x", "y", "area")
  )
  tables <- list(dist = dist, segs = segs, obs = obs, pred = pred)
  tables <- tables[!vapply(tables, is.null, logical(1))]
  for (nm in names(tables)) {
    miss <- setdiff(required[[nm]], names(tables[[nm]]))
    rec(paste0(nm, ": required columns"), length(miss) == 0,
        if (length(miss)) paste("missing:", paste(miss, collapse = ", ")) else "")
  }
  if (any(vapply(names(tables), function(nm) !all(required[[nm]] %in% names(tables[[nm]])), logical(1)))) {
    return(cl$result(stop_on_fail))
  }

  for (nm in intersect(names(tables), c("dist", "segs", "obs"))) {
    rec(paste0(nm, ": plain data.frame (not sf)"), !inherits(tables[[nm]], "sf"),
        "drop the geometry with sf::st_drop_geometry()", level = "WARN")
  }
  unit_cols <- unlist(lapply(names(tables), function(nm) {
    cols <- names(tables[[nm]])[vapply(tables[[nm]], inherits, logical(1), "units")]
    if (length(cols)) paste0(nm, "$", cols)
  }))
  rec("no units-class columns", length(unit_cols) == 0,
      paste(c(unit_cols, if (length(unit_cols)) "(convert with as.numeric())"), collapse = " "))

  rec("dist: object IDs unique", !anyDuplicated(dist$object), sprintf("%d duplicated", sum(duplicated(dist$object))))
  rec("obs: object IDs unique", !anyDuplicated(obs$object), sprintf("%d duplicated", sum(duplicated(obs$object))))
  rec("segs: Sample.Label unique", !anyDuplicated(segs$Sample.Label),
      sprintf("%d duplicated", sum(duplicated(segs$Sample.Label))))
  rec("obs -> dist: every object has a detection", all(obs$object %in% dist$object),
      sprintf("%d not in dist", sum(!obs$object %in% dist$object)))
  rec("dist -> obs: every detection is linked to a segment", all(dist$object %in% obs$object),
      sprintf("%d not in obs (they only inform the detection function)", sum(!dist$object %in% obs$object)),
      level = "WARN")
  rec("obs -> segs: every Sample.Label exists", all(obs$Sample.Label %in% segs$Sample.Label),
      sprintf("%d not in segs", sum(!obs$Sample.Label %in% segs$Sample.Label)))

  eff <- as.numeric(segs$Effort)
  rec("segs: Effort > 0", !anyNA(eff) && all(eff > 0), sprintf("%d missing or <= 0", sum(is.na(eff) | eff <= 0)))
  dd <- as.numeric(dist$distance)
  rec("dist: distances >= 0", !anyNA(dd) && all(dd >= 0), sprintf("%d missing or negative", sum(is.na(dd) | dd < 0)))
  if (!is.null(truncation)) {
    rec("dist: distances within truncation", all(dd <= truncation, na.rm = TRUE),
        sprintf("%d beyond %.0f m (will be excluded)", sum(dd > truncation, na.rm = TRUE), truncation), level = "WARN")
  }
  rec("segs: coordinates present", !anyNA(segs$x) && !anyNA(segs$y),
      sprintf("%d missing", sum(is.na(segs$x) | is.na(segs$y))))

  if (!is.null(covariates)) {
    miss <- setdiff(covariates, names(segs))
    rec("segs: covariate columns", length(miss) == 0, paste(miss, collapse = ", "))
    na <- vapply(intersect(covariates, names(segs)), function(v) sum(is.na(segs[[v]])), numeric(1))
    rec("segs: covariates complete", all(na == 0), paste(names(na)[na > 0], na[na > 0], sep = " = ", collapse = ", "))
  }

  if (!is.null(pred)) {
    p <- if (inherits(pred, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(pred) else pred
    rec("pred: coordinates and area complete", stats::complete.cases(p[, c("x", "y", "area")]) |> all())
    if (!is.null(covariates)) {
      miss <- setdiff(covariates, names(p))
      rec("pred: covariate columns", length(miss) == 0, paste(miss, collapse = ", "))
      na <- vapply(intersect(covariates, names(p)), function(v) sum(is.na(p[[v]])), numeric(1))
      rec("pred: covariates complete", all(na == 0), paste(names(na)[na > 0], na[na > 0], sep = " = ", collapse = ", "))
    }
    # Segments and grid must share a coordinate system: their extents must overlap.
    overlap <- function(a, b) max(min(a), min(b)) < min(max(a), max(b))
    rec("segs and pred in the same coordinate system", overlap(segs$x, p$x) && overlap(segs$y, p$y),
        sprintf("segs x %.0f to %.0f, pred x %.0f to %.0f", min(segs$x), max(segs$x), min(p$x), max(p$x)))
  }

  cl$result(stop_on_fail)
}

title: Estimating the detection function
text:
Not every animal within the searched strip is seen. The detection function describes how the probability of detecting an animal decreases with distance from the flight line, and it is what lets us correct counts for the animals that were missed (Buckland et al. 2001). In this article we fit candidate detection functions to the RMNP sightings, with and without covariates, and select one to carry forward into the density surface model.
The approach follows the detection function part of the dsm example A simple DSM analysis: Gulf of Mexico dolphins. The main difference is that we pool several species and let species enter the detection function as a covariate, since elk, deer and bison were seen too rarely to support separate models.

Model selection

all_models <- c(list(df_hn, df_hr, df_hn_cos), unname(df_cov))

title: Estimating abundance and its uncertainty
text:
Variance estimation
The uncertainty in abundance comes from both stages of the model: the detection function and the density surface. The dsm package offers two ways to combine them.

Variance propagation (dsm_var_prop()) refits the GAM with the detection function’s uncertainty included (Bravington et al. 2021). It requires the count response, which in turn requires detection covariates that are constant within a segment, such as weather or observer.
The delta method (dsm_var_gam()) estimates the GAM variance and adds the detection function’s coefficient of variation (CV), assuming the two are independent: \(\text{CV}_\text{total}^2 = \text{CV}_\text{GAM}^2 + \text{CV}_\text{detection}^2\).

Our detection covariates, species and the canopy cover at each sighting, vary between animals within the same segment. We therefore use the abundance.est response and the delta method.

var_moose <- dsm_var_gam(dsm_moose, pred.data = pred_df, off.set = pred_df$area)

title: Estimating abundance and its uncertainty
text:
Abundance of all species
The same steps give totals for every species. We report the estimate, its standard error and coefficient of variation, and a 95% confidence interval based on a log-normal distribution, which keeps the lower limit above zero.

abundance_row <- function(species, model) {
  s <- summary(dsm_var_gam(model, pred.data = pred_df, off.set = pred_df$area))
  N <- s$pred.est
  cv <- s$cv
  C <- exp(qnorm(0.975) * sqrt(log(1 + cv^2)))
  rhs <- sub(" + offset(off.set)", "", deparse(formula(model)[[3]]), fixed = TRUE)
  data.frame(Species = species, Model = rhs,
             N = round(N), Density_km2 = round(N / area_km2, 3),
             SE = round(s$se), CV = round(cv, 3),
             Lower95 = round(N / C), Upper95 = round(N * C))
}

title: Survey designs with subplots
text:
A crewed aircraft can fly transects across a whole study area in one or a few long flights. A drone is limited by its endurance and by how far it may fly from its operators. One practical design is therefore to divide the effort into subplots: compact blocks, each small enough to survey in one flight, with transects placed inside them. The Alberta simulation study compared such designs for fixed-wing drones and quadcopters with the conventional segmented grid design, matching the total length of transect flown (Multi-platform simulations).
The dsims examples cover designs across whole regions and designs with strata that divide a region completely (Grouped strata). This article shows how to generate subplots automatically, turn them into a region with one stratum per subplot, place systematic and zigzag transects inside them, and restrict the simulated population to the subplots. We compare them with two designs across the whole park: the conventional segmented grid of 10 km transects, which the following articles use as their default, and systematic lines with the same effort as the 2025 survey.

Coverage grid

A design across the whole park
The 2025 survey flew 3756 km on effort over the park. As a baseline, we use systematic north–south lines across the whole park with the spacing that gives the same effort: the park area divided by the line length.

title: Survey designs with subplots
text:
Designing subplots

Number and size of subplots
Each subplot is one flight. The Superwake SW-117 flies about 367 km in a 6-hour flight at 17 m/s, so the number of subplots is the total effort divided by one flight’s length. Within a subplot the lines are spaced twice the truncation distance apart, so the searched strips of neighbouring lines meet without gaps or overlap.

FLIGHT_LENGTH_M <- 17 * 6 * 3600 # 367.2 km per flight
n_plots <- round(effort / FLIGHT_LENGTH_M)
spacing_sub <- 2 * TRUNCATION_M
c(n_plots = n_plots, spacing = spacing_sub)

 n_plots  spacing 
 10.0000 522.3025 


find_best_block_dim() finds the subplot shape closest to a square that fits a whole number of lines at this spacing within each subplot’s share of the effort.

find_best_block_dim <- function(total_length, number_blocks, spacing) {
  block_length <- total_length / number_blocks
  possible_lines <- seq(1, block_length / spacing, 1)
  tibble(
    nr_lines = possible_lines,
    y_length = block_length / possible_lines,
    x_length = spacing * possible_lines,
    difference = abs(block_length / possible_lines - spacing * possible_lines)
  ) |>
    filter(total_length >= y_length * nr_lines * number_blocks) |>
    arrange(difference) |>
    slice(1)
}

plot_dim <- find_best_block_dim(effort, n_plots, spacing_sub)

Placing the subplots
To spread the subplots evenly, we use make.coverage() in a different role: asked for a given number of grid points, it places them evenly over a region. We place the centres in the park shrunk by 1 km, so no subplot is centred right at the boundary.

inner <- make.region(region.name = "inner", shape = st_buffer(region@region, -1000), units = "m")

make.coverage() can return one or two more points than requested. We build a rectangle around each centre, clip it to the park, and keep the n_plots largest.

make_subplots <- function(centres, width, height) {
  xy <- st_coordinates(centres)
  polys <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(xy)), function(i) {
    st_polygon(list(cbind(
      xy[i, 1] + c(-1, 1, 1, -1, -1) * width / 2,
      xy[i, 2] + c(-1, -1, 1, 1, -1) * height / 2
    )))
  })
  st_sf(geometry = st_sfc(polys, crs = st_crs(centres)))
}

plots <- make_subplots(centres, plot_dim$x_length, plot_dim$y_length) |>
  st_intersection(st_geometry(region@region))
plots <- plots[order(st_area(plots), decreasing = TRUE)[seq_len(n_plots)], ]
plots$ID <- sprintf("plot%02d", seq_len(nrow(plots)))



Subplots as a region
In dsims, each subplot becomes a stratum of a new region. Transects are then generated separately within each stratum.

We compare two designs within the subplots. Systematic parallel lines fill each subplot as planned. An equal-spaced zigzag (eszigzag) reduces the flying time between lines, because the aircraft does not have to turn back at the end of each line. We give the zigzag the same line length per subplot as the systematic design, taken from one set of systematic transects.

  region = sub_region, transect.type = "line", design = "eszigzag",
  line.length = transects_sys@line.length, design.angle = 0, edge.protocol = "minus",
  truncation = TRUNCATION_M, coverage.grid = cover

Coverage and effort
run.coverage() repeats the transect generation and summarises coverage, line length and total flight distance across repetitions. We use 100 repetitions per design, run in parallel (run.parallel is available in the dssd fork).

set.seed(2025)
design_full <- run.coverage(design_full, reps = 100, run.parallel = TRUE)
design_sys <- run.coverage(design_sys, reps = 100, run.parallel = TRUE)
design_zz <- run.coverage(design_zz, reps = 100, run.parallel = TRUE)
design_seg <- run.coverage(design_seg, reps = 100, run.parallel = TRUE)

The design statistics distinguish three distances: line.length is the length of transect on effort; trackline adds the travel between transects; and cyclictrackline adds the return from the last transect to the start. Coverage (p.cov.area) is the percentage of the region inside the searched strips.

design_metrics <- function(design, name) {
  s <- design@design.statistics
  data.frame(
    design = name,
    on_effort_km = s$line.length["Mean", "Total"] / 1000,
    trackline_km = s$trackline["Mean", "Total"] / 1000,
    cyclic_km = s$cyclictrackline["Mean", "Total"] / 1000,
    on_effort_pct = 100 * s$line.length["Mean", "Total"] / s$cyclictrackline["Mean", "Total"],
    covered_pct = s$p.cov.area["Mean", "Total"]
  )
}

  design_metrics(design_sys, "subplots, systematic"),

Less effort than planned. The subplot designs fly about 14% less transect than planned, because the park boundary clips some subplots. This was a common difficulty in the Alberta study as well: fixed-size subplots rarely fit an irregular study area exactly.

Restricting the population to the subplots
dsims estimates density for the region it is given. A design confined to subplots cannot provide an estimate for the whole park, so the population in the simulation must also be confined to the subplots: the estimates are then compared with the true density inside the subplots. We therefore cut the moose density grid to the subplots, label each piece with its subplot as the stratum, and set the number of groups in each stratum to its expected abundance under the DSM divided by the mean group size.

density_moose <- densities$Moose
cells_sub <- st_intersection(density_moose@density.surface[[1]], plots) |>
  mutate(strata = ID) |>
  select(strata, density, x, y)

Warning: attribute variables are assumed to be spatially constant throughout
all geometries

density_sub <- density_moose
density_sub@density.surface <- list(cells_sub)
density_sub@region.name <- sub_region@region.name
density_sub@strata.name <- sub_region@strata.name

Defining the populations
Aerial surveys detect groups rather than individuals: a group of five elk is one detection. We therefore simulate groups, with sizes drawn from a zero-truncated Poisson distribution whose mean is the observed mean group size of each species.

seen <- dist[dist$size > 0 & dist$Species %in% SIM_SPECIES, ]
group_size <- tapply(seen$size, seen$Species, mean)[SIM_SPECIES]
round(group_size, 2)

Moose  Deer   Elk 
 1.52  1.59  2.67 


When a population has a size covariate, N in make.population.description() is the number of groups, so we divide the DSM abundance by the mean group size. fixed.N = TRUE gives every simulated population exactly that many groups, placed in proportion to the density grid.

N_groups <- round(N_animals / group_size)
pop_descs <- lapply(SIM_SPECIES, function(s) {
  make.population.description(
    region = region, density = densities[[s]],
    covariates = list(size = list(distribution = "ztruncpois", mean = group_size[[s]])),
    N = N_groups[[s]], fixed.N = TRUE
  )
})
names(pop_descs) <- SIM_SPECIES
data.frame(animals = round(N_animals), mean_group_size = round(group_size, 2), groups = N_groups)
